text: Write the sealed syntax tree and a walk over it that the compiler checks for exhaustiveness. Fill in the three blanks.
choices: record Bin(char op, Expr left, Expr right) implements Expr { }
System.out.println(show(new Bin('+', new Num(2), new Bin('*', new Num(3), new Num(4)))));
answer: sealed interface Expr permits Num, Bin { }|case Num n -> String.valueOf(n.value())|show(b.left())
explanation: Verified: `(+ 2 (* 3 4))`. There is no `default` clause and none is needed — the interface is sealed, so the compiler knows there are exactly two shapes. Add a third and every walker becomes a compile error listing what to update, which on a tree walker is the difference between a safe refactor and a search. That is Chapter 22's exhaustiveness doing the job it exists for.
